narrative:
The model estimates a 47% chance that you will leave your job, which is high enough for the company to deny your promotion as a precaution.

Three factors stood out most in the decision. First, your total years of experience across all jobs pushed the prediction strongly toward staying. At 1-5 years you fall into the most common group among employees expected to remain, yet the model still saw this shorter track record as a reason you might not stay long-term. Second, having received other job offers while working here pulled the prediction toward leaving. This is relatively uncommon—only 23% of employees predicted to stay had outside opportunities—suggesting the model views external interest as a clear sign you may depart. Third, working in the “other” sector also nudged the outcome toward leaving. This sector is less common among stayers than medical or education roles, so it added to the concern.

Taken together, these points outweighed many positive signals such as your master’s degree, high salary, bonus, recognition, and overall job satisfaction.

The organization should discuss your career goals openly and explore whether additional responsibilities or clearer growth paths could reduce the risk of losing you. You, in turn, may want to reflect on how outside opportunities align with your long-term plans here. Addressing these areas now could change the outlook for both sides.
